summary: Describes generic requirements for provider provisioned virtual private networks, split into service, provider and engineering requirements. They apply to all PPVPN technologies. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3809 lists requirements for virtual private networks that service providers manage. It covers what customers should receive, what providers need to operate the service, and what network designs must support.

subtitle: Common requirements for provider-run Layer 2 and Layer 3 virtual private networks.

tldr.problem: Provider Provisioned VPNs can use different technologies, but customers and providers need a common set of requirements that applies across those technologies.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC groups requirements into customer-visible service needs, provider needs such as scaling and management, and engineering needs for forwarding, control, and interoperability.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational requirements framework for Layer 2 and Layer 3 PPVPNs, not a design for one VPN technology.

facts.label: Deployment scenarios
facts.value: Single provider/single AS, single provider/multiple ASes, multiple providers

today: RFC 3809 is an Informational RFC published in June 2004. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; it states generic requirements rather than selecting a VPN technology.

sections.title: Scope and Deployment Choices
sections.content:
A Provider Provisioned Virtual Private Network (PPVPN) connects customer sites over a shared network that a service provider helps manage. RFC 3809 gives requirements that apply to both Layer 2 and Layer 3 PPVPN technologies.

The RFC considers a single provider within one autonomous system, one provider across multiple autonomous systems, and multiple cooperating providers. It organizes requirements as service, provider, and engineering requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: A provider-run VPN connects customer sites over shared network equipment. This RFC sets common requirements across Layer 2 and Layer 3 designs and across different provider arrangements.

sections.title: Services Customers Can Check
sections.content:
Customers should be able to check whether a VPN provides the service they need. The RFC covers availability during network failures, stability during changes, unicast and preferably multicast or broadcast traffic, isolation between VPNs, addressing, and quality of service.

VPNs must support both IPv4 and IPv6. Customer traffic and routing information must remain within the relevant VPN unless the organizations have agreed to an intranet or extranet. The RFC also describes service-level objectives and the need for providers to measure and report whether they are met.
sections.plainLanguage: A VPN should keep working through failures, carry the required traffic, and keep each customer's traffic separate. Customers and providers also need a way to measure the service they agreed on.

sections.title: Provider Scale and Management
sections.content:
Providers need a VPN design that is cost-effective at both small and large scales. The RFC says a solution should address many scaling dimensions, including the number of VPNs, sites, routes, and configuration changes it can support, and should describe its limits.

Providers must be able to view VPN topology and operating state. Customers should be able to view and, after authentication and authorization, manage information about their own VPN. The RFC recommends standards-based management interfaces wherever feasible.
sections.plainLanguage: A provider needs to understand the capacity and limits of a VPN design, from small services to large ones. Customers should be able to see and manage their own service after they are authorized.

sections.title: Forwarding and Control Planes
sections.content:
The forwarding plane carries customer packets; the control plane distributes information used to establish VPN connectivity. PPVPN designs should keep VPN-specific state out of backbone routers where possible and should not require new functionality in those core devices.

The RFC calls for mechanisms that limit the spread of VPN control information, reuse common Internet mechanisms where appropriate, and preserve stability, scaling, and interoperability. It also says a solution must not interfere with backbone traffic engineering and management.
sections.plainLanguage: Customer packets must stay in their VPN, while routing and setup information must go only where it is needed. The provider's core network should not need to store details for every VPN.

sections.title: Security Across Provider Networks
sections.content:
The RFC requires VPN solutions to address customer data security, access control, site authentication and authorization, and denial-of-service attacks. Solutions should state which security features they support and how those features can be configured.

Security is especially challenging when a VPN spans multiple providers. The RFC says providers need cooperation and agreements about service levels and trust. It also notes that provider-edge equipment needs protection because attacks on it can affect VPN and Internet services.
sections.plainLanguage: VPN providers must protect customer traffic and control access to sites and network resources. When a service crosses providers, the providers need agreements about trust and service responsibilities.
